source_text:
1.6 Ἵππου τιθασία Σπάνιος ὥσπερ ἐν ἀνδράσιν
οὑτωσὶ δὲ καὶ ἐν ἵπποις εἰλικρινής ἐστιν ἀρετή. Ἐγγὺς γὰρ τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς κακία
βάσκανος, ἵνα μὴ τὸ κα λὸν καθαρὸν φανῇ· λόγιός τις, ἀλλ' οὐ σεμνός· καὶ ἄλλος
στρατηγεῖ μέν, ἀλλ' οὐ σωφρονεῖ· καί τις ἀνδρεῖος, ἀλλ' ἀλαζὼν ἄχραντον οὐκ
ἐφύλαξε τὸ κάλλος αὑτῷ· καὶ ἄλλος ἄλλῳ πλεονεκτεῖ τε καὶ ἁμαρτάνει. Ὅμοια καὶ
τὰ ἐφ' ἵππων καλὰ καὶ πονηρά· ταχεῖς, ἀλλ' ἐρωτικοί, θηρευταί, ἀλλὰ στομίαι,
βαδισταί, ἀλλ' ὑβρισταί· τοὺς ἀναβάτας ἄλλοι οὐ δέχονται, οἳ δὲ ἀποσείονται·
παρατρίβουσιν ἔνιοι τοίχοις ἢ φυτοῖς· οἳ μὲν ἐκ φύσεως κακοῦργοι, οἳ δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν
κεκτημένων γεγενημένοι, δάκνουσι καὶ λακτίζουσι καὶ ἀφίστανται καὶ
ἀναχαιτίζουσιν, ἢ μισοῦντες ἢ ὑπερηφανοῦντες τοὺς δεσπότας. Καὶ πολλοὺς εἰπεῖν
ἔχω, ἄλλον ἄλλῃ συμφορᾷ καὶ εἴδει κακῶν ποικίλως ὑφ' ἵππων διεφθαρμένους.
Τέχναι μὲν οὖν πωλοδαμνῶν ὡς οἷόν τε τὰς κακίας ἢ ἐπέχουσιν ἢ διορθοῦσιν,
ὀλιγοσιτίᾳ τοὺς ὑβριστάς, ἐκτομῇ τοὺς ἐραστάς, κημοῖς τοὺς δάκνοντας, τοὺς
στομίας λύκοις, πληγαῖς τοὺς ἀπειθεῖς. Τί δ' ἄν τις ποιήσειεν κατὰ τοῦ ἀφεστηκότος
καὶ πείθεσθαι μηδενὶ τρόπῳ ἐς μηδὲν μήτε ἐπιταγμάτων μήτε μαθημάτων
προῃρημένου; Ὥσπερ γὰρ τὰ ἀγριώτατα τῶν θηρίων τέλεια ληφθέντα οὐ
τιθασσεύεται, ἀλλά, κἂν πρὸς ὀλίγον χειροήθη γεγενῆσθαι δοκῇ, ὅμως τῆς πρόσθεν
ὠμότητος οὐκ ἐπιλανθάνεται, οὑτωσὶ δὲ καὶ τόδε τὸ θρέμμα δυσμετάγωγον, κακίας
ἐγχρονισθείσης. Ἐπεὶ τοίνυν ἀσθενὴς πρὸς τὰ τοιαῦτα πληγὴ καὶ ἀπειλὴ καὶ τέχνη
καὶ τροφή, κακία φύσεως τέχνῃ φύσεως διορθούσθω. Ἡμερωσάτω αὐτὸν καὶ γραφή,
ἣν οὐ φοβηθήσεται, ἣν οὐχ ὑποπτεύσει, ἣν φορῶν δαμασθήσεται. Κοίλῳ ὁπλῆς
προτέρου ποδὸς εὐωνύμου, χειρὶ εὐωνύμῳ ἐγχάραττε γραφίῳ χαλκῷ, σελήνης
ἑκκαιδεκαταίας, Ῥωμαίας προσταγῆς ἀπειλήν· ἀνάγκην ἔχει πειθαρχίας ἡ γραφή·
κεῖται δὲ ἐν ʹ πενταγώνῳ, ᾧπερ ἐγγέγραπται ὑπάτων διατόνου σημεῖα, φῖ καὶ
δίγαμμα.
pass_a_gloss: Horse-taming. Rare as among men, so also among horses is unmixed virtue. For next to the good things is a grudging vice, in-order-that the fine may-not appear clean: one is eloquent but not grave; another generals but is-not temperate; someone is brave but a braggart did-not-keep the beauty unstained for himself; and another in another thing both has-the-advantage and misses. Like also the on-horses fine-things and bad: swift but lustful, hunters but hard-mouthed, walkers but violent; some do-not receive the riders, others shake-them-off; some rub against walls or plants; some from nature are mischief-makers, others have-been-made so by the owners; they bite and kick and stand-off and rear, either hating or despising the masters. And many I can-tell, another by another disaster and form of evils variously destroyed under horses. Arts then of colt-tamers as-far-as-possible either check or correct the vices: scant-food the violent, castration the lovers, muzzles the biters, wolf-bits the hard-mouthed, blows the disobedient. But what would someone do against the one-that-has-stood-off and has-chosen to-obey in no manner toward nothing either of commands or of lessons? For just-as the wildest of beasts taken full-grown are-not-tamed, but even-if for a little they seem to-have-become handy, still they do-not-forget the former savagery, so also this creature is hard-to-turn, vice having-grown-old-in-it. Since then toward such things blow and threat and art and feeding are weak, let vice of nature by an art of nature be-corrected. Let a writing also tame him, which he will-not fear, which he will-not suspect, which wearing he will-be-broken. In the hollow of the hoof of the front left foot, with left hand, engrave with a bronze graver, of a sixteenth-day moon, a threat of a Roman command; the writing has a necessity of obedience; it lies in the [blank-numeral] pentagon, in-which have-been-written signs of the high diatonic, phi and digamma.
pass_b_english: Taming a horse. Unmixed virtue is rare among men, and so also among horses. Next to the good things sits a grudging vice, so that the fine may not appear clean. One man is eloquent but not grave; another generals but is not temperate; someone is brave, but being a braggart he did not keep beauty unstained for himself; and another in another thing both has the advantage and misses. The fine and the bad in horses are like that: swift but lustful, hunters but hard-mouthed, walkers but violent. Some will not take riders; others shake them off. Some rub against walls or plants. Some are mischief-makers by nature, others have been made so by their owners. They bite and kick and stand off and rear, either hating or despising their masters. I can tell of many, each destroyed in a different disaster and form of evils under horses.

The arts of colt-tamers, as far as they can, either check or correct the vices: scant food for the violent, castration for the lovers, muzzles for the biters, wolf-bits for the hard-mouthed, blows for the disobedient. But what would a man do against the one that has stood off, and has chosen to obey in no way, toward nothing, either of commands or of lessons? Just as the wildest beasts, taken full-grown, are not tamed, but even if for a little they seem to have become handy they still do not forget the former savagery, so also this creature is hard to turn once vice has grown old in it.

Since then blow and threat and art and feeding are weak toward such things, let a vice of nature be corrected by an art of nature. Let a writing also tame him — a writing he will not fear, will not suspect, and wearing which he will be broken. In the hollow of the hoof of the front left foot, with the left hand, engrave with a bronze graver, on a sixteenth-day moon, a threat of a Roman command. The writing has a necessity of obedience. It lies in the pentagon whose numeral is blank in the lock, in which have been written the signs of the high diatonic: phi and digamma.

choices.why: λύκος in tack is the wolf-toothed bit; pairing it with στομίας (hard-mouthed horses) is equipment, not feeding them to wolves.

anf_compare.notes: No PD English of the Cesti body; ANF has the letters only.
